cards.front: What is a .dmg file in macOS?
cards.back: An Apple Disk Image - similar to an ISO file. When mounted, it appears as a virtual drive in Finder.

cards.front: What is a .pkg file in macOS?
cards.back: An installer package - runs a script-based installation process. macOS equivalent of Windows setup.exe.

cards.front: What is a .app file in macOS?
cards.back: An application bundle - not a single executable but a folder containing all the app's files. Right-click > View Package Contents to see inside.

cards.front: How do you uninstall most apps on macOS?
cards.back: Drag the .app file from the Applications folder to the Trash. Deleting the bundle removes all app files. Some apps include a separate Uninstaller.app - run that instead.

cards.front: macOS equivalent of Windows Program Files?
cards.back: /Applications folder.

cards.front: What does ~ (tilde) represent in macOS paths?
cards.back: The current user's home directory. For example, ~/Library = /Users/username/Library.

cards.front: What is /Library vs ~/Library in macOS?
cards.back: /Library - system-wide support files (scripts, fonts) shared by all users and apps. ~/Library - per-user library, hidden by default in Finder.

cards.front: Where are macOS operating system files stored?
cards.back: /System - equivalent to the Windows System32 area.

cards.front: What is a Managed Apple ID?
cards.back: A corporate/education Apple ID managed through Apple Business Manager. Can integrate with Active Directory and MDM for central device management.

cards.front: Time Machine backup schedule?
cards.back: Hourly backups for the past 24 hours. Daily backups for the past month. Weekly backups for all previous months. Deletes oldest when volume fills.

cards.front: What is Rapid Security Response (RSR) in macOS?
cards.back: Emergency security patches pushed immediately for critical vulnerabilities. On by default. A letter suffix on the OS version (e.g., 14.1.1a) means an RSR was applied.

cards.front: macOS equivalent of the Windows Control Panel?
cards.back: System Preferences (called System Settings in newer macOS versions).

cards.front: Where is FileVault enabled in macOS?
cards.back: System Preferences > Privacy and Security > FileVault.

cards.front: macOS equivalent of Windows BitLocker?
cards.back: FileVault - full disk encryption using the login password or iCloud credentials.

cards.front: macOS equivalent of Windows File Explorer?
cards.back: Finder - file management front end for launching apps, managing files, and accessing network shares.

cards.front: How do you launch Spotlight search in macOS?
cards.back: Command+Space. Or click the magnifying glass in the upper-right corner of the desktop.

cards.front: What is Mission Control in macOS?
cards.back: Shows all running apps spread across the desktop for quick navigation. Activate with 3-finger swipe up or Control+Up arrow.

cards.front: What are Spaces in macOS?
cards.back: Multiple virtual desktops managed from within Mission Control. Each Space can have its own set of running apps.

cards.front: What is Keychain in macOS?
cards.back: Built-in encrypted credential store. Stores passwords, certificates, and secure notes. Decrypted with the user's login password. Not an add-on - it is integrated into macOS.

cards.front: What is Continuity in macOS?
cards.back: Feature that lets you hand off tasks between macOS, iPadOS, and iOS devices. Includes: pick up where you left off, iPhone as Mac webcam, AirDrop, text message forwarding. Requires iCloud login on all devices.

cards.front: What is Disk Utility in macOS?
cards.back: Graphical tool for managing file systems. Format drives, create/modify partitions, mount/unmount volumes, create disk images.

cards.front: How do you Force Quit a hung app in macOS?
cards.back: Command+Option+Escape (opens Force Quit window). Or: hold Option, right-click the app in the dock > Force Quit.

cards.front: What is iCloud Drive?
cards.back: Apple's cloud file storage service - similar to Google Drive or Dropbox. Files stored in iCloud Drive are accessible from all Apple devices signed into the same Apple ID.

cards.front: Where is the macOS command line accessed?
cards.back: Terminal app. Provides a shell (bash/zsh) for running scripts and managing the OS.
